newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia mediator welcomes Serb comments.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia mediator welcomes Serb comments.

text.p: International mediators said on Tuesday they welcomed signs that Serb leaders were ready to attend meetings of Bosnia's newly-elected presidency and parliament after boycotting an inaugural ceremony.
The Serb member of the collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Serb parliament deputies refused to show up to the ceremony in Sarajevo's national theatre on Saturday.
They alleged the venue was "unsafe" for Serb representatives and objected to the wording of an oath to Bosnian statehood.

But after Western powers condemned the Serbs for their boycott, Krajisnik said on Monday he was prepared to cooperate and would recommend that Serb deputies sign an oath pledging to uphold the Bosnian constitution.
"If he means what he says we believe this is a good sign, it's to be welcomed," Colum Murphy, a spokesman for the office of the High Representative, Carl Bildt, told a news conference.
"But on the other hand we will adopt a wait and see attitude and wait to see that he actually makes that contact," Murphy said.
Krajisnik said in an interview that he and other Serb representatives were willing to support the "solemn declaration" which Moslem and Croat deputies signed in Saturday's ceremony.
"I have the intention that I should send this to the other representatives of the assembly and, if they agree, that we should sign it at a ceremony," he told the BBC.

The High Representative, who oversees civilian aspects of the Dayton peace treaty, castigated Serb hardline nationalists for pulling out of the parliamentary session at the last moment after negotiating details of the ceremony for several days.
Murphy said that it was up to Krajisnik and the Serb leadership to initiate the next meeting of the parliament and the three-man presidency, elected on September 14.
Krajisnik and his Moslem and Croat counterparts, Alija Izetbetgovic and Kresimir Zubak, held the first session of the three-man presidency a week ago.

"We believe that Mr Krajisnik has our telephone number and that of his colleagues. And we would expect that he would get in touch with presidents Izetbegovic and Zubak so that there is no further delay in these most important matters," Murphy said.
He also hinted that the Serbs risked losing reconstruction aid if they failed to participate in meetings of newly-elected joint institutions.
Bosnian Serb leaders, whose army laid siege to Sarajevo during 43-months of war, have been reluctant to set foot in the city centre for government meetings, citing safety concerns.

Krajisnik has proposed holding presidency and parliament sessions in a number of alternative venues, including the outskirts of Sarajevo near Serb-held territory, at the city's shell-pocked airport or foreign embassies.
